meaning: Something a program can run out of, such as a core's arithmetic units, memory bandwidth or memory latency. The resource a program runs out of first is its bottleneck, and it sets the program's speed.
A small program that we ran in place of one of the arm's real jobs. Its results carry over to that job only if the job has the same bottleneck.
The physics engine that runs the simulated scenes in this dive. One step advances a scene by one timestep.
The set of event counters inside a processor core. It counts events such as clock cycles, stalled slots and retired micro-operations.
The record of one program on one core. It holds the program's rate, its four slot shares and its memory stall.
The Linux tool that reads the PMU counters over one run of a program.
A lower internal precision for float32 matrix multiplies on NVIDIA GPUs that still gives a float32 result. PyTorch allows it when you call torch.set_float32_matmul_precision("high").

What perf does when it cannot count every requested event at the same time. Each event is counted for part of the run and its total is scaled up, so a ratio of two events that were not counted together can lose accuracy.

A method that finds a core's bottleneck from its event counters. It sorts every slot into one of four categories, retiring, front-end bound, back-end bound and bad speculation, and reports each category as a share of all slots.

A fetch of data into one of the core's caches, the first-level data cache or the second-level cache, from further out in the memory system. The number of refills per thousand instructions shows how heavily a program depends on memory.

Arm's counters that split a top-down share into its causes. For example, STALL_BACKEND_MEMBOUND, counted together with STALL_BACKEND, separates back-end stalls caused by memory from those caused in the core. Our runs did not count them.
The name under which Linux exposes the PMU of one core type, such as armv8_pmuv3_1 for the Cortex-X925 on a DGX Spark. You name perf events through it.
The Linux command that pins a program to chosen cores. Pinning makes sure the counters come from one known core type.
A small loop built to exercise one resource of a core, such as its multiply-add units or its memory.
One chance, in one clock cycle, for a core to start one micro-operation. Each core has a fixed number of slots per cycle.
One of the small steps a core splits an instruction into. Slots start micro-operations, and the back end executes them.
The number of slots a core has per cycle. It is 10 on the Cortex-X925 and 5 on the Cortex-A725. On the Cortex-A78AE it is 6, a figure we derived from the core's own counters.
The share of slots that started a micro-operation whose result the program kept.
A core predicting which way a branch goes and starting the instructions beyond it before it knows the answer.
Throwing away the work a core started after a wrong prediction, and restarting on the right path.
The share of slots spent on work that the core threw away after a wrong prediction, and on the restart after it.
The share of slots left empty because the front end of the core, which fetches and decodes instructions, had no micro-operation ready.
The share of slots left empty because the back end of the core, which executes micro-operations, could not accept another one.
The share of clock cycles in which the back end waited for data from memory. It comes from a separate counter, read in a second execution of the program.

The number of instructions a core finishes, divided by the clock cycles it takes. A core's throughput equals its instructions per cycle times its clock rate, divided by the instructions one unit of work takes.
Arm's adjustment that moves the cycles a core spends recovering from a flush out of front-end bound and into bad speculation.
The event and formula definitions that Arm publishes for each core, including its top-down formulas and its slots per cycle. Arm publishes no file for the Cortex-A78AE.
The number of bytes per second that memory can stream to a core.
The time one isolated read from memory takes.
One instruction that computes a x b + c. A loop of independent scalar fused multiply-adds measures a core's multiply-add throughput without its vector units.
A loop that streams through arrays larger than the caches. It measures memory bandwidth.
A loop in which each read gives the address of the next read. It measures memory latency.
The core's cache of address translations. A pointer chase over a large area also pays for its misses.
Arm's vector instructions, which work on several numbers at once.
The function that sets negative values to zero. It is applied after a layer of a neural network.
The interface MuJoCo uses for hardware-accelerated rendering without a display.
One function launched on the GPU.
NVIDIA's profiler for a single GPU kernel. It reports compute throughput and memory throughput as shares of the GPU's maximum.
One of the GPU's processing units. A GPU repeats it many times across the chip.
The GPU's general execution path, which does not use the tensor cores.
The GPU units built for the matrix arithmetic of neural networks.
The p50 is the median time per call. The p99 is the time that only one call in a hundred exceeds.
AWS's own family of Arm processors. Their cores are Arm Neoverse designs.
The imitation-learning policy of section 4. It predicts a chunk of future actions.
A small vision-language-action model, from the policy family covered in section 5.
The latent world model covered in section 7.
NVIDIA's GPU telemetry tool. It samples the activity of the GPU's units over time.
The Jetson's built-in monitor. It reports processor, GPU, memory and power readings, including the GPU clock.
NVIDIA's timeline profiler. It shows when the GPU works and when it waits.
